title: Data hiding
relevance: SDE interviews check whether candidates can separate encapsulation from data hiding and design class interfaces that keep object state valid.

phases.goal: Define encapsulation vs data hiding and name the three C++ access levels and their defaults.

must_hit.point: Encapsulation bundles data and functions into one class; data hiding is the security policy that restricts who can access or modify internal state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States bundling as encapsulation and access restriction via access specifiers as data hiding, not treating them as synonyms.

must_hit.point: By default, members of a class are private; members of a struct are public.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly contrasts class private default with struct public default.

must_hit.point: C++ visibility is controlled by the three access specifiers public, private, and protected, written as labels followed by a colon.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three specifiers and that they label sections of the class body.

probes: What is the difference between encapsulation and data hiding?
What is the default access for members of a C++ class versus a struct?

hints.1: Think about bundling versus who is allowed to touch the internals.
hints.2: Encapsulation is the single-entity package; data hiding uses access specifiers like private.
hints.3: A class with entirely public members is still encapsulated, but its data is not hidden; class defaults to private, struct to public.

phases.goal: Explain what each specifier allows and how getters/setters mediate private state.

must_hit.point: private members are reachable only by the class's own member functions; public members form the interface reachable by anyone; protected members act like private to the outside world but like public to derived classes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the three reachability rules, including protected as inheritance middle ground.

must_hit.point: An accessor (getter) retrieves a member and should be marked const to promise it will not modify the object; a mutator (setter) changes a value and can validate or update related state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pairs getter with trailing const and setter with validation or related-state updates.

must_hit.point: An access specifier applies to all members declared below it until the next specifier or the end of the class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes section-scoped labels rather than per-member keywords only.

probes: Who can access private, public, and protected members?
Why mark a getter const, and what does a setter give you that direct field access does not?

hints.1: Map each specifier to outside code, the class itself, and derived classes.
hints.2: private = own methods only; public = anyone; protected = derived like public, outsiders like private.
hints.3: Getters end with const and only read; setters are the place to reject invalid values before assigning private fields.

phases.goal: Explain why data is hidden and how getter/setter choices set property permissions.

must_hit.point: If data is public, external code can break invariants, couple to internals so implementations cannot change, and prevent easy access tracking when values change anywhere.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three problems: broken invariants, coupling to internals, and no access tracking.

must_hit.point: Property permissions are chosen by which public methods you expose: both get and set for read-write, only get for read-only, only set for write-only.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists read-write, read-only, and write-only in terms of providing getters and/or setters.

must_hit.point: Python data hiding is mainly a naming convention such as _variable, while C++ enforces access control at compile-time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts convention-only hiding with compile-time enforcement in C++.

probes: What goes wrong if all fields are public?
How would you make a field read-only versus write-only using accessors and mutators?

hints.1: Consider validity rules, future refactors, and debugging who changed a value.
hints.2: Public balance can be set invalid; public raw storage locks the implementation; direct writes are hard to intercept.
hints.3: Read-only = getter only; write-only = setter only (e.g. password hash); C++ rejects illegal access at compile time unlike Python underscores.

phases.goal: Apply hiding with validated setters and controlled account operations, and nail the classic interview distinction.

must_hit.point: A Rectangle can keep length and breadth private and reject invalid setter input so a negative breadth is not stored as a negative size.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes private dimensions plus setters that only accept non-negative values (or reset invalid input).

must_hit.point: A BankAccount can expose accountNumber as read-only via a getter with no setter, and change balance only through controlled actions like deposit rather than a free public field.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions getAccountNumber without a setter and deposit-style updates instead of public balance writes.

must_hit.point: A class whose members are all public is still encapsulated as a bundle, but its data is not hidden.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the all-public class as the precise counterexample separating encapsulation from data hiding.

probes: How would you design Rectangle or BankAccount so clients cannot put the object into an invalid state?
Is a class with only public members encapsulated? Is its data hidden?

hints.1: Put state private and route changes through methods that check rules.
hints.2: Use setters or domain methods for writes; omit setters when a value should not change after construction.
hints.3: Encapsulation = bundled class; data hiding = private/protected with controlled public interface—all-public members fail the hiding part.

tradeoffs.topic: Public data members vs private members with accessors/mutators
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Public fields let callers break invariants, freeze the internal representation, and scatter writes with no single place to log or breakpoint; private fields plus getters/setters keep a stable interface while validation and implementation can change behind it.

tradeoffs.topic: Read-write vs read-only vs write-only properties
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Expose get and set for read-write; expose only get for values set once or computed internally; expose only set in rare cases like passwords where plaintext must not be readable back.

tradeoffs.topic: Encapsulation without data hiding vs encapsulation with access control
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Bundling alone (even all-public members) is encapsulation; adding access specifiers such as private supplies the security policy that actually hides and protects state.

gotchas.trap: Treating encapsulation and data hiding as the same concept.
gotchas.correction: Encapsulation is bundling data and behaviour into one entity; data hiding is the benefit of restricting access with specifiers like private. An all-public class is encapsulated but not data-hidden.

gotchas.trap: Assuming C++ hides members the way Python does with a leading underscore.
gotchas.correction: In Python, underscore naming is a convention; C++ access control is enforced at compile-time.

gotchas.trap: Making data members public and treating that as the class interface.
gotchas.correction: Reserve public for the interface methods clients should call; keep almost all data members private so invariants and internals stay under the class's control.
